bib.title: Inference Pipeline Deployment (Chapter 10), LLM Engineer's Handbook
bib.venue: Packt (book chapter; read from O'Reilly print, ISBN 9781836200079)

question: How should an LLM inference pipeline be designed and deployed (deployment type, monolith vs microservices, SageMaker, autoscaling)?
contributions: Compares online real-time, asynchronous and offline batch deployment
Argues for splitting LLM service from business logic
Walks through deploying a fine-tuned 8B LLM Twin on AWS SageMaker with the Hugging Face TGI DLC and a FastAPI RAG service
Explains SageMaker autoscaling (scalable target, target-tracking policy, cooldown)

results.claim: Latency and throughput couple by 1/latency for unbatched serving: 100 ms per request gives 10 RPS, 10 ms gives 100 RPS.
results.quote: if the service takes 100 ms to process requests, this translates to a throughput of 10 re‐ quests per second.

results.claim: With batching, higher latency can mean higher throughput: 20 requests in 100 ms is 200 RPS.
results.quote: if you process 20 batched requests in 100 ms, the latency is 100 ms, while the throughput is 200 requests per second.

results.claim: 60 requests in 200 ms is 300 RPS, so doubling latency raises throughput by half.
results.quote: If you process 60 requests in 200 ms, the latency is 200 ms, while the throughput rises to 300 requests per second.

results.claim: Async queue example: 2 VMs absorb a jump from 10 to 100 RPS without scaling out.
results.quote: the number of requests spiked to 100 requests per second. Instead of scaling the number of virtual machines (VMs) by 10, which can add drastic costs, the requests are queued, and the same two VMs can process them in their rhythm without any failures.

practices: Decide deployment type from throughput, latency, data and infrastructure requirements (Criteria for choosing deployment types).
Use real-time inference for chatbots; async for spiky or long jobs; batch when delayed predictions are acceptable (Understanding inference deployment types).
Use gRPC for internal services and REST for public APIs (Online real-time inference).
Start monolithic but keep ML and business logic in separate modules or packages so a later split is cheap (Choosing between monolithic and microservices).
Split the LLM service (GPU) from the business service (CPU) so each scales and uses hardware independently (Microservices architecture).
Use identical preprocessing and post-processing in training and inference to avoid training-serving skew (The training versus the inference pipeline).
Create a narrow IAM user and execution role for the deployment instead of using an admin account (Configuring SageMaker roles).
Delete SageMaker resources after testing to avoid growing costs (Calling the endpoint / FastAPI section).
Autoscale with target tracking, set min >= 1 and a max, and use cooldowns; avoid over- and under-scaling by stress testing in a dev environment (Autoscaling).

the time it takes for a system to process a single inference request from when it is received until the result is returned.
